Reclaim the City

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Social Housing and the evictions of poor inner city residents is a political hot potato for the City of Cape Town and Reclaim the City, a social movement of residents, is making sure they keep the pressure on City officials to deliver.
Possibly their most successful campaign is the occupation of two former Provincial hospital buildings, forcing the City of Cape Town to negotiate with them. Although they are owned by the Province, the City has to provide alternative housing before they can be evicted. The former Woodstock Hospital is now home to 800 people and the former nurse’s residence of Somerset Hospital at the Waterfront is home to 500 families. Unlike many derelict buildings occupied by people across all cities in South Africa, these buildings are run by elected leaders who are residents and active members of Reclaim the City.


Further information:
Bevil Lucas lives in the old matron’s office in the Woodstock hospital. A resident of Woodstock for the past 30 years, his family own a house down the road, but after his divorce he could find nowhere to live in the area. As an elected leader he heads up the residents’ committee that manages the facility now known as the Cissy Gool Building. He is organising two other residents to speak to us.
An indication of how formally these houses are run, before people can move into Cissy Gool they are vetted and have to agree to the house rules of no drug or alcohol abuse. They also have a 1am curfew and children have to be indoors and out of the corridors by curfew. They have established a vegetable garden from which they provide a Friday meal. It’s a community of people from all races and ages, all former residents of the area. Currently their futures are a bit more stable as Reclaim the City won a court case against the City to prevent their eviction while the City works out the way forward.
Across town is the Helen Bowden Nurses’ Home. The former nurses’ residence of the Somerset Hospital at the Waterfront is home to 500 families. Elizabeth Gqoboko, a carer in the area and former domestic worker, is one of the original and elected leaders of Helen Bowden. She along with four other women formed Reclaim the City, and occupied the derelict nurses’ home when the City sold the Tafelberg School site, which was the only land earmarked for social housing in Sea Point, to a private developer. Now 500 families have taken up residence. Elizabeth is finding two other residents to tell us their story.
These two occupation highlight the massive need for social housing and the impasse the City is in in releasing City-owned land in the inner City. Reclaim the City’s report on City leases, which highlighted 23 properties across the City leased to private owners for R1,000 each per annum (including 18 golf courses), once again put the City in the spotlight. Deputy Mayor Ian Neilson has made numerous commitments to social housing, saying Green Point Bowling Green was one such site. Putting pressure on Neilson to keep his word, Reclaim the City built a wall on the site on May Day
The City of Cape Town has promised social housing on inner City land for decades, but has failed to deliver anything since 2008 when discussions began with activist and NGO groups. With the gentrification of Woodstock and Salt River, many residents who had lived there for generations started losing their homes. A group of activists who were residents in these communities got together and took occupation of the two sites in 2017.
The City, recognising the need for social integration and social housing, allocated 11 parcels of City-owned land in the Woodstock/Salt River area for families. But the process of this development has been extremely slow and gets bogged down by four different pieces of legislation - Zoning applications, heritage applications, water use licences and environmental impact assessments.

Press Release:


Reclaim the City
A political hot potato or media savvy social movement that is redefining how the needs of the poor can be met in city spaces? Hundreds of indigent residents have staged an orderly occupation of prime real estate in Cape Town's Waterfront precinct and are now calling rooms formerly used as nurses’ residences their home. Carte Blanche meets the social movement Reclaim the City that is forcing the City of Cape Town to find ways to negotiate with them and ensure that prime locations are not only for the wealthy.
Producer: Liz Fish
Presenter: Masa Kekana


Script:


Link: Apartments are popping up all over Cape Town and at 1.5 million you can get yourself a bachelors pad and that is considered a bargain it can cost R17 000 a month to rent a two bedroom in a fairly average apartment here in Sea Point. This despite endless promises and protests, Cape Town City Centre still remains the home for the rich.
Script: And accused of being the most unintegrated in the country
Elizabeth “I never thought in my whole life since moving to Cape Town that I wouldn't be one of the tenants that today to stand on a balcony facing and living next to the Waterfront…
Script: 3 years ago, Elizabeth Gqoboka along with 500 people, occupied the former Nurses home of Somerset Hospital near the Waterfront, which is owned by Department of Public Works. She has been a carer in Seapoint for the past 28 years. When we last spoke to her she was living in a tiny room, fighting to stop the sale of the Tafelberg property, which had been earmarked for affordable housing. When that fell through, although it was illegal, Reclaim the City activists searched for a Government building to occupy.
Masa “How did you find this building.
Elizabeth “This building has been standing vacant since 2015 Since we moved here the Province actually cut the electricity. Most of the areas in the building vandalized like this. When we came here. If you can see a lot of pipes have been cut off by people it was stripping off some copper.
Script: So for 3 years, they have been collecting their water from two taps outside the building, but as an elected leader she uses the fire hydrant on her floor, but the building is pitch dark
Upsound “The scariness doesn't only come at night when you are on your own and other people are at work
Script: Almost everyone living here has a story to tell of rising rents, evictions by developers, or body corporates.
Zisanda “I don’t want to live anywhere else I have been born and bred here there should be affordable houses I don’t want to be promised a better place out somewhere else this is my home
Script: Zisanda and her sister were born in Sea Point, sharing this tiny room with their father Wilson who works here as a caretaker. When she was in Grade 10, they were evicted, only her father could stay on the property
Wilson” I was not sleeping at night I was always thinking about my kids because I never live in location, since I move to Cape Town I always live in Sea Point up until now. My kids were born here I raised them here. All of a sudden they have to move to location- they didn’t cope
Script: Wilson and his daughters were one of the first families to occupy the nurses home, which they renamed Ahmed Kathrada House
Wilson “The reason we are doing what we are doing is we want affordable houses
Script: The Department of Public Works owns this building, but if they were to act on the illegal occupation, by law, the City has to find alternative accommodation. And to date that’s been Blikkiesdorp and Wolwerivier, 30 kms outside the city, both are virtually full.
Elizabeth “There's no public transport systems there's no shopping centers, there is no schools there's no clinics and then we decided no this is totally not on.
Script: Currently Reclaim the City has occupied 5 government buildings across town, all getting legal advice from the Ndifuna Ukwazi Law Centre. Director Mandisa Shandu says the review of the decision to sell the Tafelberg school will be heard in September this year
Mandisa “ It's a testimony of people not being able to wait anymore for promises that are not met and simply taking a stand, and acting in some ways as civil disobedience, to say that well unless and until you act on these commitments you don’t have anything else or anywhere else to go.
Script: The biggest and possibly the most organised occupation is of the former Woodstock hospital, renamed Cissy Gool House. Since 2017 Bevil Lucas has been one of the elected leaders.
Bevel “A group of us got together to look at the issue of homelessness and how we could take up the campaign around the spatial development in the area as gentrification was really taking off
Script: 800 people live here from different cultural backgrounds, anyone whose facing eviction and homelessness
Bevel” If the person is accepted is the person asked to undertake to participate in the life of the organization here in the occupation.
Script: Adamo and Kathleen live here with their two children, having moved all over Woodstock trying to find a room they could afford, but as a foreigner Adamo kept losing his job. Kathleen runs the crèche, and as a skilled handyman, Adamo spends a lot of his day maintaining the hospital
Adamo “Now at least we have a place we can call home. For me really this is the first time I have lived in a place and feel at peace.
Mandisa “ there's not been one affordable housing unit that's been built in the post Apartheid era in a well located areas. Housing is being delivered but on the periphery doesn't change the social fabric of the city. And I think that all levels of government are implicated in that fact
Malusi “They want to create this narrative that the City of Cape Town is not committed to social housing which is false
Script: Mayoral Committee Member for Human Settlements Councillor Malusi Booi took over the portfolio 6 months ago
Malusi “We have we have huge plans and one of one of the sites is this particular site that will give us a yield of more than 600 units. We're also looking at one of the projects in Mowbray. It's one of the golf courses. it will give us a good yield because it will also be next to the Conradie project that we're currently doing with the province and that has a yield of more than 3000 units
Script: This week they moved 75 people from a local informal settlement into the first Transitional housing. Booi says this is the first step to unlock the 11 social housing projects promised in 2017 by the City.
Malusi”You will ask me when are we going to get a building on this site. But what what we're doing we need to assess this site we need to make sure that there's rezoning. Environmental assessments that on its own takes you to about 18 months. Just on that particular process
Link: “Ndifuna Ukwazi recently published a report in which they highlighted 24 properties leased by the City to various sporting bodies for as little as R1000 per annum year, all in prime locations ideal for affordable housing and largely under used.
Script: On May Day Reclaim the City staged a symbolic protest at the Green point bowling club reminding the City that they said it was ideal for social housing
Malusi “That was an act of criminality. So I cannot engage in that fashion. If people want to engage. They must come to my office.
Script: The other site of protest was Rondebosch Golf Club, 450,000m2 of public land, the equivalent of 90 rugby fields, directly opposite the King David Mowbray Golf Club, also on public land. Close to public transport, hospitals and schools, and just 10 kilometers outside the City
Mandisa “These are areas that we are saying you ought to have a different imagination about how this land is used. Not just only for necessary affordable housing but the building of mixed income communities that would go a long way in terms of having a more inclusive kind of city.
Malusi “To manage some of their facilities they pay more than five million. So you need to you need to understand it holistically. That particular site because it's a wetland for us to be able to develop that site it would take us huge sums of money. Hence we look at other parcels of land that we have earmarked that are developable.
Link: In January this year the residents of Woodstock Hospital won their eviction case taking advantage of the Constitutional Court ruling that prevents people from eviction if it makes them homeless. The compromise with the City is that there is now a register of all the occupiers, and no new residents are allowed to move in.
Bevil” What been very exciting is it from an acrimonious type position to one as the city has referred to it as co-operative. So we are quite positive we will get to a solution
Script “Woodstock hospital is owned by the Province, so first the City had to get power of attorney before assessing the site with their engineers. They hope to redevelop it into 700 affordable housing units. However no indication has been given to the occupants at the nurses home”
Zisanda “I feel very disappointed actually basically that is one of the reasons I didn’t even vote because everyone promises us the same things but no one delivers it”
Script: The department of Public works said they would install solar lights and while we were there, they came and cut the grass and cleaned up.
Elizabeth “ If we can sustain being tenants in this house is gonna be like each and every person that never had a house will eventually own a house and that’s the victory

Close to public transport, hospitals and schools, and just 10 kilometers outside the City Mandisa “These are areas that we are saying you ought to have a different imagination about how this land is used. Not just only for necessary affordable housing but the building of mixed income communities that would go a long way in terms of having a more inclusive kind of city. Malusi “To manage some of their facilities they pay more than five million. So you need to you need to understand it holistically. That particular site because it's a wetland for us to be able to develop that site it would take us huge sums of money. Hence we look at other parcels of land that we have earmarked that are developable. Link: In January this year the residents of Woodstock Hospital won their eviction case taking advantage of the Constitutional Court ruling that prevents people from eviction if it makes them homeless. The compromise with the City is that there is now a register of all the occupiers, and no new residents are allowed to move in. Bevil” What been very exciting is it from an acrimonious type position to one as the city has referred to it as co-operative. So we are quite positive we will get to a solution Script “Woodstock hospital is owned by the Province, so first the City had to get power of attorney before assessing the site with their engineers. They hope to redevelop it into 700 affordable housing units. However no indication has been given to the occupants at the nurses home” Zisanda “I feel very disappointed actually basically that is one of the reasons I didn’t even vote because everyone promises us the same things but no one delivers it” Script: The department of Public works said they would install solar lights and while we were there, they came and cut the grass and cleaned up. metadata.Summary: Social Housing and the evictions of poor inner city residents is a political hot potato for the City of Cape Town and Reclaim the City, a social movement of residents, is making sure they keep the pressure on City officials to deliver. Possibly their most successful campaign is the occupation of two former Provincial hospital buildings, forcing the City of Cape Town to negotiate with them. Although they are owned by the Province, the City has to provide alternative housing before they can be evicted. The former Woodstock Hospital is now home to 800 people and the former nurse’s residence of Somerset Hospital at the Waterfront is home to 500 families. Unlike many derelict buildings occupied by people across all cities in South Africa, these buildings are run by elected leaders who are residents and active members of Reclaim the City.
metadata.Further information: Bevil Lucas lives in the old matron’s office in the Woodstock hospital. A resident of Woodstock for the past 30 years, his family own a house down the road, but after his divorce he could find nowhere to live in the area. As an elected leader he heads up the residents’ committee that manages the facility now known as the Cissy Gool Building. He is organising two other residents to speak to us. An indication of how formally these houses are run, before people can move into Cissy Gool they are vetted and have to agree to the house rules of no drug or alcohol abuse. They also have a 1am curfew and children have to be indoors and out of the corridors by curfew. They have established a vegetable garden from which they provide a Friday meal. It’s a community of people from all races and ages, all former residents of the area. Currently their futures are a bit more stable as Reclaim the City won a court case against the City to prevent their eviction while the City works out the way forward. Across town is the Helen Bowden Nurses’ Home. The former nurses’ residence of the Somerset Hospital at the Waterfront is home to 500 families. Elizabeth Gqoboko, a carer in the area and former domestic worker, is one of the original and elected leaders of Helen Bowden. She along with four other women formed Reclaim the City, and occupied the derelict nurses’ home when the City sold the Tafelberg School site, which was the only land earmarked for social housing in Sea Point, to a private developer. Now 500 families have taken up residence. Elizabeth is finding two other residents to tell us their story. These two occupation highlight the massive need for social housing and the impasse the City is in in releasing City-owned land in the inner City. Reclaim the City’s report on City leases, which highlighted 23 properties across the City leased to private owners for R1,000 each per annum (including 18 golf courses), once again put the City in the spotlight. Deputy Mayor Ian Neilson has made numerous commitments to social housing, saying Green Point Bowling Green was one such site. Putting pressure on Neilson to keep his word, Reclaim the City built a wall on the site on May Day The City of Cape Town has promised social housing on inner City land for decades, but has failed to deliver anything since 2008 when discussions began with activist and NGO groups. With the gentrification of Woodstock and Salt River, many residents who had lived there for generations started losing their homes. A group of activists who were residents in these communities got together and took occupation of the two sites in 2017. The City, recognising the need for social integration and social housing, allocated 11 parcels of City-owned land in the Woodstock/Salt River area for families. But the process of this development has been extremely slow and gets bogged down by four different pieces of legislation - Zoning applications, heritage applications, water use licences and environmental impact assessments.
